content.p: Sam Bankman-Fried founded the cryptocurrency exchange FTX and the trading firm Alameda Research. In November 2023 a Manhattan jury convicted him on all seven criminal counts, after deciding that he had secretly diverted FTX customers' money to Alameda. On 28 March 2024 Judge Lewis Kaplan sentenced him to 25 years in prison and ordered him to forfeit $11 billion.

His convictions were upheld on appeal on 12 June 2026. On 10 September 2026 his lawyers asked the US Supreme Court for a new trial, and a separate request for a presidential pardon is listed as pending. He has maintained that he is not guilty.

FTX filed for bankruptcy on 11 November 2022, when it ran out of money in what the Associated Press called the cryptocurrency equivalent of a bank run. According to City AM, the trouble began after a public quarrel between Bankman-Fried and Changpeng Zhao, the head of the rival exchange Binance. Zhao ordered the sale of almost $600 million of FTX tokens and then agreed to buy FTX, subject to checks, before withdrawing within 24 hours. CNN described the sequence differently: a leaked balance sheet showing how closely Alameda was tied to FTX set off a panic among investors and customers. Binance later said FTX's problems were beyond its ability to help.

On the evening of 12 December 2022 the Royal Bahamas Police Force arrested Bankman-Fried in the Bahamas. The Bahamian Attorney General's office said the arrest followed formal notice that the United States had filed criminal charges and was likely to seek extradition. US Attorney Damian Williams said the arrest was based on a sealed indictment from his office. It came a day before Bankman-Fried was due to testify to the House Financial Services Committee.

The indictment, announced on 13 December 2022, contained eight counts, according to CNN. The Justice Department's release listed them as wire fraud conspiracy and wire fraud (two of each), commodities and securities fraud conspiracies, a money laundering conspiracy, and a conspiracy to defraud the Federal Election Commission and break campaign finance rules. Williams said the case was "not a case of mismanagement or poor oversight, but of intentional fraud, plain and simple." He pleaded not guilty. The Justice Department's release carried the standard reminder that an indictment is only an allegation.

In February 2023 Judge Kaplan temporarily tightened Bankman-Fried's bail conditions after prosecutors found that he had sent a text message to FTX's former general counsel, who was named in court papers as "Witness-1." In the message he wrote that he would like to "see if there's a way for us to have a constructive relationship." Kaplan wrote that it appeared to be an effort to have the two men "sing out of the same hymn book," and found a "material threat of inappropriate contact with prospective witnesses."

By August 2023 the judge had concluded that Bankman-Fried had tried to influence Caroline Ellison and other likely witnesses. He was jailed, ending his confinement to his parents' home in Palo Alto, California, under a $250 million bond, according to the Associated Press.

Prosecutors told jurors that Bankman-Fried took FTX customer deposits for his own use, to make investments, to make political donations to candidates from both parties, and to repay billions of dollars Alameda owed. The Justice Department said he also gave Alameda's lenders false financial statements, inflated FTX's revenue and profits in figures given to investors, and backdated contracts.
The prosecution relied heavily on three people who had worked closest to him and who had pleaded guilty. NPR reported that most of them had lived together in a $30 million penthouse in the Bahamas.

Ellison, Alameda's chief executive and Bankman-Fried's on-and-off girlfriend, testified under a cooperation deal. "He directed me to commit these crimes," she told the court, according to the Associated Press. She said Alameda had withdrawn up to $14 billion from FTX, some of it later repaid, and that political donations included $35 million channelled to Republican candidates through one operative and $10 million that Bankman-Fried steered towards Joe Biden. CNN reported her testimony that before the collapse FTX owed its clients $12 billion but held only $4 billion for them, and that she sent lenders "dishonest" balance sheets.

Gary Wang, FTX's co-founder and chief technology officer, testified that his job was to turn Bankman-Fried's vision into code. According to NPR, he said small changes to that code let Alameda take as much as $65 billion from FTX customers without their knowledge. Nishad Singh, FTX's chief engineer, told the court that at Bankman-Fried's direction he wrote code that effectively let Alameda borrow tens of billions of dollars from FTX.

Bankman-Fried testified in his own defence, saying he never intended to defraud anyone. The jury deliberated for less than five hours before convicting him, Bloomberg reported. The Justice Department listed the verdicts as two counts of wire fraud, two of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and one each of conspiracy to commit securities fraud, commodities fraud and money laundering. The campaign-finance conspiracy count in the original indictment is not among them.

At the sentencing on 28 March 2024, prosecutors asked for 40 to 50 years. The defence, led by Marc Mukasey, asked for five to six and a half years and described Bankman-Fried as an awkward maths nerd rather than a "ruthless financial serial killer." Assistant US Attorney Nicolas Roos told the court the collapse was not a liquidity crisis or an act of mismanagement but "the theft" of billions of dollars of customer money.

Sunil Kavuri, a customer who lost money in the collapse, told the court he had suffered every day for two years. Bankman-Fried apologised and said "My useful life is probably over," but also suggested that customers would eventually get their money back and blamed the bankruptcy court for the delay. Kaplan said that in 30 years on the federal bench he had "never seen a performance" like Bankman-Fried's testimony, which was, in his words, either outright lying or evasive. He said he had never heard "a word of remorse for the commission of terrible crimes," and that there was a risk "this man will be in a position to do something very bad in the future."

The judge rejected the argument that there was no loss because the bankruptcy estate expected to repay customers, calling it "misleading, logically flawed and speculative." He sentenced Bankman-Fried to 25 years, about half of what prosecutors wanted, and ordered the $11 billion forfeiture, which the government may use to compensate victims. The Justice Department put the stolen customer money at more than $8 billion. Kaplan recommended a medium-security or lower prison, ideally near San Francisco so his family could visit. A former federal prosecutor, Mitchell Epner, told CNN that with all available credit for good behaviour he could serve as little as 12.5 years.
Ellison, Wang and Singh had pleaded guilty and testified for the government. Bloomberg reported that Wang and Singh avoided prison and that Ellison received two years.

Bankman-Fried's appeal argued that Kaplan wrongly stopped the defence from telling jurors there was plenty of money to repay FTX customers, and that he barred any claim that Bankman-Fried had relied on lawyers' advice. His lawyers also accused the judge of repeatedly putting "a thumb on the scale" for the government, according to Bloomberg. His appeals lawyer, Alexandra Shapiro, said the defence was "cut off at the knees." The Second Circuit heard oral argument in November 2025.

On 12 June 2026 a three-judge panel unanimously affirmed the convictions, the sentence and the forfeiture in a 42-page opinion by Judge Parker, with Judges Lee and Araújo Kahn. It held that even temporary misappropriation violates the fraud statute. "FTX customers were defrauded as soon as Bankman-Fried transferred their money to Alameda regardless of how strongly he believed he might later return the money," Parker wrote. The court relied in part on the Supreme Court's 2025 decision in Kousisis v. United States, which held that a person commits fraud by using a material lie to get someone to hand over money or property, whether or not he meant the victim to lose money, according to the newsletter Citation Needed.

The panel found that Bankman-Fried was able to give the jury his version of events when he testified about his good faith belief that Alameda's assets exceeded its liabilities. On the advice-of-counsel point it found no error, noting that the FTX lawyers had not been told all the relevant facts. It also rejected his challenges to the jury instructions and to the forfeiture. The panel acknowledged that $11 billion was a very large amount where many victims might eventually be made whole, but Lawyer Monthly reported that it held the forfeiture statute looked to the defendant's gains rather than his moral culpability.
content.h2: Fights that came after the verdict
content.p: In February 2026 Bankman-Fried asked for a different judge to hear a motion for a new trial, claiming that Kaplan had shown "extreme prejudice." The motion alleged that the Justice Department under President Biden had threatened witnesses into silence or into changing their testimony. In March 2026, prosecutors questioned whether he had written an extension request himself, days after his mother, Barbara Fried, sent a letter to the court on his behalf. In April he withdrew the motion, without prejudice to renewing it later, saying he did not expect a fair hearing from Kaplan. Fortune later reported that a federal judge denied his motion for a new trial in April.

The pardon request is a separate track. Bankman-Fried applied for a pardon from President Donald Trump, which Fortune reported was listed as pending on the Justice Department's website on 8 June 2026. Another outlet gave the filing date as 8 June. Citation Needed noted that it was for a pardon "after completion of sentence," which would not shorten his term. Trump said in a January 2026 interview that he had no plans to pardon him, and a White House spokesperson pointed Fortune to those remarks. In July 2026 the US Senate unanimously adopted a resolution opposing clemency, led by Cynthia Lummis and Ruben Gallego, according to Unchained. It cannot prevent a pardon.

On 10 September 2026 his lawyers, reportedly including the Stanford law professor Jeffrey Fisher, filed a petition for certiorari asking the Supreme Court for a new trial and to strike down the forfeiture. They argue that jurors should not have heard evidence of customer losses when the defence could not show the assets were there to repay them, and that the $11 billion forfeiture violates the Eighth Amendment's ban on excessive fines. "All the more so where the truth is the victims did not lose money," Fisher told CNN. Unchained noted that the court accepts about 1% of the thousands of petitions it receives each term; Crypto Briefing added that a decision on whether to hear the case was expected later in 2026.

The FTX Recovery Trust announced a fifth distribution of about $900 million to creditors from 31 July 2026. Cointelegraph reported that the trust had paid out about $10 billion since the bankruptcy, and that convenience claims under $50,000 would receive 120% under the plan, with other claimants receiving 103% to 105%. The defence team points to this as evidence that customers were repaid, according to Crypto Briefing. Judge Kaplan had called the same expectation speculative at sentencing, and the Second Circuit ruled that later gains on assets Bankman-Fried bought were irrelevant to whether he committed fraud.

Bankman-Fried remains in federal custody. Reports on where have differed: Bloomberg described a low-security prison near Los Angeles, Fortune named Terminal Island, where Michael Avenatti shared his cell, and Cointelegraph said he was housed at Lompoc in April 2026.
